KEY MESSAGE 1...A strong cold front is expected to cross 
through the region today, resulting in widespread showers and 
thunderstorms. Flash flooding, damaging wind gusts and a few 
tornadoes are possible later 
today.

To the south of a closed upper low over eastern Canada, broad 
troughing will be in place across much of the Northeast and Mid-
Atlantic. An embedded mid-level shortwave will pass through the
base of the trough today. At the surface, a warm front will 
move into portions of the area tonight as a cold front will 
begin to approach the area on Thursday.

With guidance coming into better agreement with the timing and 
placement of frontal boundaries in our area, there has been an 
uptick in confidence in what the evolution of what should
transpire later today. Multiple rounds of widespread showers 
and storms are expected. With the cold front approaching from 
the west, and a warm front expected to set-up across the 
southern half of the area across the Delmarva and into southern 
New Jersey, we will have to watch these areas for severe weather
this afternoon and evening. 

Bulk shear values up to 30-40 kt support organized clusters 
where locally damaging wind gusts are possible. Some of the 00z 
CAMs have been suggesting some isolated discrete supercells 
developing out ahead of the main batch of convection. Thinking 
the models may have a good idea of how things will evolve today,
with scattered showers and thunderstorms starting out as 
individual discrete cells in the early afternoon with a more 
linear, multi-cell clusters taking over and pushing through by 
the mid-afternoon and into the early evening.

With the warm front draped over portions of the area, 
there will be a localized corridor of a tornado threat, 
especially where any storm is able to latch onto the boundary. 
SPC has introduced a 5% tornado risk over SE PA, northern 
Delaware, and the southern half of New Jersey. Locally backed 
flow at the surface near/south of the warm front will enhance 
low-level shear. In addition to increased low-level shear, we 
will have a very moist airmass overhead and low LCLs - factors 
favorable for tornadogenesis. Some question remains in how far 
north the warm sector gets, which will have implications for 
where the largest tornado threat is. For now though, the 
forecast currently has the area south of the PA Turnpike and 
I-195 as the main area to watch. This does include the Philly 
metro area. Cannot rule out isolated large hail as well as 
temperatures aloft are rather cool for this time of year. Cloud
cover should increase at the morning goes on, which could be a
limiting factor in terms of instability buildup. The Slight 
(2/5) Risk remains for most of the area.

The other, and possibly more concerning threat may be the risk 
and potential for flash flooding across portions of the area. 
Most guidance continues to depict a very moisture rich airmass 
surging northward today where PWAT values are expected to top 
out around 2.2-2.6 inches. Model forecast soundings also show 
tall, skinny CAPE profiles and a relatively deep warm cloud 
layer. The one saving grace is that the overall shear vectors 
indicate that storms should be 'relatively' quick moving. 
However, any given storm will be capable of producing highly 
efficient rain rates, at times around 2 to 4 inches per hour. 
With this being said, WPC has maintained a SLIGHT risk (Level 
2/4) for excessive rainfall today over most of the area. There
was talk of adding a Moderate Risk around the Philly metro, but
have held off for now. Added Morris County, NJ to the Flood
Watch since there was a slight trend north with the highest QPF.
Otherwise, no changes. The Flash Flood Watch remains in place
for most of New Jersey, southeastern PA, and northern Delaware. 

In general, expecting anywhere between 1 to 2 inches of rain to
fall, with localized higher amounts up to 3 to 5 inches.
Guidance has remained relatively consistent all throughout
today. We will have efficient rainfall producers where some
areas could see multiple rounds, which is not a good
combination. This event will also be during the evening commute,
with travel disruptions likely. Have multiple ways to receive
warnings. 

The severe and flooding rain threat should diminish overnight 
into Friday morning.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Conditions look to remain unsettled through the
weekend, with daily chances of showers and storms each day.

Mid to long range NWP and AI guidance suggests that the pattern
could become unsettled Friday night and into the weekend. 
The cold front will move offshore tonight but stall just
offshore. Multiple waves of low pressure will ride along the
stalled front, resulting in unsettled weather through the
weekend. The main periods to watch are early Saturday through
Saturday evening, with periods of rain increasingly likely,
especially along/east of the I-95 corridor. Another round of
rain is expected on Sunday as well. The severe threat looks low
